## Abstract

Orthostatic intolerance is a category of disorders characterized by inadequate

adjustment to hemodynamic changes upon standing. leading to increased risk of fainting,

elevated heart rate, and other morbidities. These symptoms lead to increased fall risk,

which is a significant source of morbidity and mortality in elderly populations. This thesis

proposes the development of a portable, active abdominal compression binder to alleviate

the severity of orthostatic intolerance. We designed and fabricated a novel active binder

that applies motor-driven abdominal compression upon the detection of standing to restore

hemodynamics and reduce symptoms.

Twenty healthy volunteers (ages 18–50 years) completed three randomized supine-

to-standing trials: no binder, a commercial passive binder, and the novel active binder.

Throughout each trial, compression pressure, heart rate, and respiration were continuously

monitored and comfort was assessed via post-trial survey. The results demonstrated that

the active binder achieved a higher mean compression pressure (≈ 11 mmHg) with

significantly lower intersubject variability (standard deviation (SD) ≈ 1 mmHg) than the

passive binder (mean ≈ 8 mmHg; SD ≈ 3 mmHg). Active compression reduced the standing

heart rate by 4.4 bpm compared to control (p<0.05), versus a 1 bpm reduction with the

passive binder (p>0.05). These findings suggest that active abdominal compression may

serve as a more efficacious, consistent, and user-friendly alternative treatment for

mitigating orthostatic intolerance.

## Introduction

Orthostatic intolerance encompasses a spectrum of disorders in which the body

struggles to maintain adequate blood flow to the brain and stable blood pressure when a

person stands upright [1-3]. Under normal physiology, standing induces a rapid

displacement of approximately 300–800 mL of blood into the abdomen and lower

extremities, which in turn activates pressure receptors in the aortic arch and carotid sinuses,

called arterial baroreceptors. These sensors trigger vasoconstriction (constriction of blood

vessels) and an increase in heart rate to restore blood pressure and maintain perfusion to

the brain [4].  When this regulatory feedback loop breaks down, whether due to reduced

sensitivity of these pressure sensors, damage to the autonomic nervous system, or stiffening

of blood vessel walls, orthostatic intolerance may develop [4, 5]. Clinically, this can

manifest as postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome (POTS), in which standing causes

the heart rate to rise by at least 30 beats per minute within ten minutes, without a significant

drop in blood pressure [6] or as orthostatic hypotension (OH), defined by a fall in systolic

blood pressure of at least 20 mmHg or diastolic blood pressure of at least 10 mmHg within

three minutes of standing, potentially leading to dizziness, blurred vision, or syncope [4].

Orthostatic intolerance syndromes affect a significant portion of the population:

POTS is estimated to afflict up to 0.5–1% of adults, predominantly young females [2, 7],

and OH prevalence ranges from 5% for those under 50 years to over 30% among adults

older than 70 years [4, 5]. Among older adults, the dizziness and syncope caused by OH

contributes substantially to fall risk; importantly, more than one in four individuals aged

65 years and older experience a fall each year, and falls are a leading cause of morbidity

and mortality in this population [8]. As both OH and POTS can lead to significant


<!-- Page 8 -->


7

morbidity and reduced quality of life, user‐friendly assistive strategies pose a significant

clinical need.

Current therapeutic strategies, including pharmacologic agents, functional

electrical stimulation (FES), compression garments, and lifestyle modifications, offer

partial relief from the symptoms of orthostatic intolerance syndromes but carry notable

drawbacks. α-Adrenergic agonists (e.g., midodrine) and mineralocorticoids (e.g.,

fludrocortisone) raise systemic vascular resistance and blood volume, respectively, but

are non‐selective, often causing high blood pressure while lying down supine

hypertension, paresthesia (tingling), pruritus (itching), and other side-effects [1, 9, 10].

Further, studies have shown that chronic hypertension, where blood pressure is broadly

elevated, is a significant risk factor for orthostatic hypotension [4]. Since the

aforementioned drugs treat orthostatic hypotension by increasing blood pressure, this

may lead to a feedback effect, whereby drugs used to treat this disorder may only further

exacerbate it in the long term. Thus, there is much interest in finding non-

pharmacological solutions that target only the period of standing in order to reduce these

undesired effects.

FES, involving lower body muscle electrical stimulation, can augment venous

return via muscle contractions but demands clinical oversight and can discomfort patients

[11, 12]. Compression garments, such as graduated stockings or abdominal binders,

mechanically counteract venous pooling and thus increase standing blood pressure in OH

patients [13, 14] and reduce the elevated heart rate in POTS [13, 15]; however, these

suffer from low patient adherence owing to difficulty donning, constant pressure

discomfort, and inconsistent application [16, 17]. Additionally, leg compression


<!-- Page 9 -->


8

stockings have been shown to be less effective in reducing the severity and duration of

OH compared to abdominal binders and leg-to-waist stockings, as the abdomen contains

a greater reserve of venous blood [18, 19]. Lifestyle measures (increased salt/water

intake, physical counter‐maneuvers) are generally adjunctive [18].

In recent years, researchers have become increasingly interested in abdominal

compression systems that automatically adjust when a person changes posture, applying

pressure when needed and releasing it when lying down, with the goals of avoiding high

blood pressure in the supine position, reducing unnecessary discomfort, and improving

long-term use. Some designs rely on the patient manually activating the device, for

example by pulling a strap or inflating a bladder upon standing [20, 21]. However, these

approaches require the user to physically engage the device and vary widely in ease of

use.

Other studies have explored fully automated compression, but these prototypes

often depend on pneumatic inflated devices that require tethering to a stationary air pump

source [22]. These devices have demonstrated clinical efficacy, but are generally

intended for hospital or laboratory settings where portability is not required, and they are

poorly suited for everyday wear or quick, on-demand use. Nevertheless, the majority of

syncopal events occurs in domestic environments [9], posing significant limitations for

these devices.

A final limitation of current research is that there is minimal literature directly

comparing the hemodynamic efficacy of adaptive abdominal compression systems

against standard abdominal binders, nor assessing their relative comfort and usability

profiles. Several important mechanistic questions remain insufficiently explored in the


<!-- Page 10 -->


9

existing body of work. In particular, it is not well understood how the magnitude of

applied compression pressure quantitatively influences physiological responses such as

blood pressure stabilization and venous return. Similarly, the role of the compression

mechanism itself remains unclear: specifically, whether compression that is dynamically

applied during upright posture confers different physiological benefits compared to

continuous, static compression, independent of overall pressure levels. Addressing these

gaps was therefore a central objective of this project, with the goal of providing a more

comprehensive understanding of how both pressure magnitude and mode of application

contribute to the overall efficacy of abdominal compression systems.

To address these limitations, we have designed a novel active abdominal

compression binder that autonomously applies selective pressure to the abdomen during

the transition to standing. The device aims to match the hemodynamic benefits of passive

binders and maintain their light-weight, portable, and low-cost design, while enhancing

comfort, ease of donning, and thus improve overall patient adherence and therapeutic

effect. The active binder applies a target abdominal compression pressure of 11 mmHg

via a motorized cord compression upon sensing upward rising motion. We evaluated the

device in a cohort of 20 healthy subjects, assessing its ability to deliver consistent

compression pressures, effectively attenuate orthostatic cardiovascular responses and

maintain patient comfort.

## Materials and Methods

Active Compression Binder Design

Structural Layout

As shown in Fig. 1a, the active binder comprises three primary components. First,

a non-contractile segment made of laminated foam fabric (Jolemina®, Parnu, Estonia)

encircles the torso and provides a comfortable interface with the body. This region is

designed for comfort, because it makes the greatest contact with bony structures in the

abdominal region, such as the hip bone and spine. Laminated foam fabric is an optimal

material for this purpose, since it maintains structural integrity and is minimally extensible,

but still provides comfortable padding. This segment attaches via Velcro to the contracting

region and can be interchanged in varying lengths (e.g., 30–50 cm) to accommodate

different body sizes.

Second, two pieces of felt provide structural stability to the front of the device and

additionally house the electronics compartment, motors, and pulley assemblies. Felt is

required for this component because it provides sufficient stiffness to maintain structural

integrity under load while still being compliant enough to conform to the body, as well as

serving as a durable substrate that can securely anchor mechanical components.

Third, a thin cotton fabric backing spans the anterior abdomen; behind this layer,

rows of strings are routed through pulley mechanisms and, when actuated, pull to

approximate the felt components and generate circumferential compression (see


<!-- Page 12 -->


11

Compression Mechanism). Together, the latter two elements form the contracting region

of the binder.

All rigid fixtures (motor housings, spool mounts, and string channels) were 3D-

printed in polylactic acid (PLA) at 15–20% infill density to balance strength and weight.

The entire active binder, including all electronic and motor components, weighs 0.29 kg.

Figs. 1b–c show the full active binder mounted on a mannequin before compression, and

*Fig. 1d shows the commercially available passive binder (Procare Health®, St. Peters, MO,*

USA).

Compression Mechanism

A single vertical column of pulleys is positioned on each side of the shortening

region. Four high-strength nylon cords are anchored to motor-driven spools. The routing

configuration is shown in Fig. 1a: two cords are guided through the central pulleys and two

through the peripheral pulleys. The pulley mechanism consists of nylon ball-bearing

pulleys housed within custom 3D-printed casings, which serve to both retain the string

within the pulley track and prevent direct contact between the pulley and the underlying

felt. To further reduce friction and wear, 0.5 mm PVC sheets with heat-activated adhesive

backing were applied to the felt beneath each pulley. Together, these design elements

facilitate smooth, low-resistance motion of the strings during actuation. Multiple narrow

fabric channels were sewn along the shortening region to guide the tensioning cords and

maintain proper alignment during actuation. When the user stands, the tightening cords


<!-- Page 14 -->


13

draw the pulley columns together, reducing the length of the shortening region and thereby

increasing the circumferential pressure applied to the abdomen.

Each cord reels onto a miniature spool, driven by a geared N20 micro-motor (100:1

gearbox, max 37 RPM; Greartisan Manufacturers®, USA). This motor was selected to

balance actuation speed with sufficient torque for effective compression. At a maximum

speed of 37 RPM and using a 3 cm diameter spool, the linear retraction speed can be

estimated as 3π×37≈ 348 cm per minute, or approximately 5 cm/s. This corresponds to a

minimum actuation time of ~3 seconds to achieve full compression, which was deemed

fast enough to respond to postural changes while remaining gradual enough to avoid

discomfort to the user. Additionally, the 100:1 gear reduction provides relatively high

maximum torque (on the order of ~1.5 kg·cm), enabling the motor to generate sufficient

tension in the cords to achieve meaningful abdominal compression without stalling under

load.

Pressure Measurement

A bladder isolated from a brachial blood pressure cuff (12 cm x 18 cm) rests directly

against the wearer’s abdomen, secured within a fabric pouch sewn onto the inner face of

the shortening region, as shown in Fig. 2. The bladder connects pneumatically to an

HX710B pressure sensor (HiLetgo®, Shenzhen, Guangdong, China) on the outside of the

felt. Uniform bladder compression by the shortened region yields real-time measurements

of applied abdominal pressure.

the membrane approaches zero, such that 𝑃𝑜𝑢𝑡≈𝑃𝑖𝑛. Accordingly, the optimal bladder

Electronics and Sensor Configuration

All electronics are controlled by an Arduino Nano® microcontroller (Arduino,

Turin, Italy). A lightweight 9V LiPo rechargeable battery provides power; a step-down

voltage regulator converts this to 6V for the actuator motors, while the Arduino and sensor

modules run at 5V via the Nano’s onboard regulator.

Motor direction and braking are managed by a DRV8833 dual H-bridge driver

(American Control Electronics®, South Beloit, IL, USA), interfaced to the Nano via 4

digital direction pins. The H-bridge supports bidirectional winding and rapid stops.

Binder activation is automated using an BMI270 inertial measurement unit (IMU),

integrating a 3-axis accelerometer and 3-axis gyroscope (HiLetgo®, Shenzhen,

Guangdong, China). The IMU is mounted on the felt. A threshold-based algorithm running

on the Nano detects the transition to an upright posture and commands the DRV8833 to

actuate the motors. Specifically, activation is triggered when the vertical acceleration

exceeds approximately 0.15 g and the velocity exceeds 3 cm/s. This threshold was

empirically tuned through iterative testing across multiple trials, during which several

combinations of acceleration and velocity criteria were evaluated. The selected parameters


<!-- Page 17 -->


16

were chosen to reliably detect physiologic sit-to-stand transitions while minimizing false

positives from minor movements or shifts in posture.

A single HX710B microelectromechanical pressure sensor measures abdominal

compression via the embedded bladder. The sensor communicates with the Arduino over

SPI at 100 millisecond intervals. Prior to deployment, we calibrated the HX710B against a

laboratory-grade digital manometer, deriving a linear scale factor to convert raw voltage to

mmHg. Calibration is only necessary during fabrication.

All modules, including the Arduino Nano, HX710B sensor breakout, DRV8833

driver, MPU6050, and power regulation circuitry, are consolidated onto a custom 4.5 × 6

cm printed circuit board (PCB) mounted on the felt base. The fully assembled electronics

package weighs 65 grams and operates untethered, supporting portable use when serial

data logging is not required.

A closed‐loop pressure control algorithm running on the Arduino Nano maintained

a target compression of 11 mmHg. The firmware continuously detected peak and trough

values over each respiratory cycle, computing the mean pressure from the previous breath.

Peak detection was implemented using a derivative-based approach, in which the rate of

change of pressure was estimated over a 250 ms moving window. Time points at which the

derivative transitioned from positive to non-positive were identified as local maxima

(peaks), while transitions from negative to non-negative were identified as minima

(troughs).


<!-- Page 18 -->

The mean pressure (𝑃𝑚𝑒𝑎𝑛) over each cycle was then subtracted from the setpoint

(𝑃𝑠𝑒𝑡) to yield an error term, defined as:

𝑒 = 𝑃𝑠𝑒𝑡  − 𝑃𝑚𝑒𝑎𝑛.

A constant voltage correction strategy based upon the error 𝑒 was used due to the

discrete operating voltage of the motors. Specifically, when (𝑒 > 0), the motors were

driven at +6 V to increase compression, and when (e < 0), they were driven at -6 V to

release compression:

𝑉𝑚𝑜𝑡𝑜𝑟 = {  −6 𝑉     𝑖𝑓 𝑒< 0

+6 𝑉    𝑖𝑓 𝑒> 0

This constitutes a basic positional control scheme with binary actuation, allowing

the system to incrementally adjust toward the desired pressure. This mechanism offers a

resolution of ~0.5 cm of compression, translating to a correction of ± 0.5 mmHg of

pressure per time step for correction. By updating control output only once per

respiratory cycle, the system minimized overcorrection and reduced oscillatory behavior.

With a 9 V, 600 mAh battery, the active binder can sustain over 5,000 cycles of a

10-second increase to maximum pressure followed by release, corresponding to repeated

sit-to-stand transitions.

Passive Binder

For comparison, a standard‐grade, commercially available abdominal binder,

which we call a “passive binder”, was modified to include pressure sensing (Fig. 1d). A

second blood‐pressure cuff bladder was positioned beneath the binder against the abdomen


<!-- Page 19 -->


18

and secured via a sewn Velcro pouch. This bladder connected to an HX710B pressure

sensor interfaced with an Arduino Nano, using the same SPI communication and

calibration procedure described above. We mounted the electronics, including the Arduino

Nano, HX710B sensor, and power regulation, in a portable enclosure, allowing for real‐

time monitoring of passive binder pressures during the study.

To evaluate the consistency, effectiveness and comfort of the active binder, a

randomized crossover study was conducted at the MIT Institute for Medical Engineering

and Science (IMES) (IRB protocol #2503001596), in accordance with the Declaration of

Helsinki. This study used a healthy-volunteer model consistent with prior work  [23, 24],

which assesses orthostatic tachycardic responses as a physiologic surrogate for venous

return. All subjects provided written informed consent prior to participation. Fig. 3 depicts

the overall protocol flow.

*Table 1. Participant Summary*

Demographic and anthropometric characteristics of the study cohort (n = 20), including

are presented as mean ± standard deviation; categorical variables are given as percentage

<!-- Page 21 -->


20

Twenty healthy adults were enrolled; participants were eligible if they were in age

range 18–50 years and had no known cardiovascular conditions, autonomic disorders, or

standing difficulties. Table 1 summarizes the key characteristics of the study’s participant

population.

After consent, each participant’s abdominal circumference was measured with a

flexible tape measure following normal expiration. Subjects then completed three trials in

randomized order—control (no binder), passive binder, and active binder—each consisting

of 1 minute supine rest followed by 2 minutes of quiet standing. Heart rate and respiratory

rate were continuously recorded via an ApneaLink Air™ (ResMed®, San Diego,

California, USA) chest-belt respiration monitor and pulse oximeter.

During passive binder trials, participants donned the binder and tightened it as per

standard instructions for the device: “as tightly as possible”. In active binder trials,

participants first adjusted the binder until it “just fit snugly,” then we verified fit by

confirming a baseline pressure of ~2-3 mmHg; those with waist circumference >80 cm

used the Velcro extender for an appropriate initial fit. If the binder was not fit properly or

the grommets were not vertically aligned (see Fig. 1a-c), the study personnel adjusted the

Velcro attachment until alignment was corrected.

All pressure and motion data from both the active and passive binder trials were

streamed over USB via the Arduino Nano’s serial interface to a laptop and timestamped on

receipt. We synchronized these timestamps with the ApneaLink Air chest-belt and pulse

oximeter data streams. At any point, participants could manually disable the device by

disconnecting an accessible power cord. The time between successive trial conditions


<!-- Page 22 -->


21

within each participant was less than 2 minutes (for donning and preparation). At the end

of the session, participants rated comfort and usability for each condition (Likert scale),

given 8 prompt questions.

Statistical Analysis

Paired t-tests were used to compare mean compression pressures, standing heart

rate, change in heart rate from supine to standing (ΔHR), and respiration rate between

active, passive, and control conditions. An F-test was used to compare the standard

deviation of compression pressures between active and passive binders. Multiple linear

regressions were applied to evaluate the influences of abdominal circumference and sex on

compression pressure, as well as to evaluate the independent effect of compression pressure

and compression mechanism (active vs. passive) on heart rate responses. For all statistical

tests, the threshold for significance was considered as p < 0.05.

## Results

Compression Pressure

For all participants, the active binder reached its peak pressure in less than 7

seconds (mean 5.1 seconds, SD 1.23 seconds). Fig. 4 summarizes the abdominal

compression pressures achieved by the active and the passive binder under full tension, as

well as the comparisons across sexes and baseline abdominal circumferences.

As shown in the gray boxplots in Fig. 4a, the active binder delivered a higher and

more consistent pressure (mean 10.9, SD 1.3 mmHg) compared to the passive binder (mean

8.3, SD 2.86 mmHg) with statistical significance (paired t-test p = 0.017, F-test p = 0.0013).

This indicates that the active system not only exceeded the maximal compression

achievable by the passive binder but did so with roughly half the variability across

participants.

When stratified by sex, the active binder produced equivalent pressures for both males

and females (mean 10.9 mmHg vs. 11.1 mmHg), whereas males fitted with the passive

binder experienced higher average pressures than females (mean 10.3 mmHg vs. 8.3

mmHg). Further, the active binder maintained consistent compression regardless of

abdominal size (linear regression p-value = 0.29), while the passive binder showed a

positive trend between abdominal circumference and applied abdominal pressure, whereby

larger waists correlated with increased pressure (linear regression p-value = 0.01) (Fig. 4b).

Tachycardic Response Across Conditions

Figs. 5a and 5b present boxplots of ΔHR and standing HR for each condition: active

binder, passive binder, and control (no binder). The active binder attenuated the increase

most effectively (mean ΔHR = 10.8 bpm, standing HR = 69.0 bpm), followed by the

passive binder (mean ΔHR = 12.8 bpm, standing HR = 72.0 bpm), and the control

condition, which elicited the largest tachycardic response (mean ΔHR = 15.9 bpm, standing

HR = 74.5 bpm). Medians follow the same order, indicating that the active device reduced

the orthostatic heart rate surge relative to both passive binder and control.

Within‐Participant Comparisons

*Fig. 5c (turquoise) depicts each subject’s pairwise differences in ΔHR: control vs.*

active (mean difference = 5.3 bpm, p = 0.0014), control vs. passive (mean = 3.3 bpm, p =

0.001), and passive vs. active (mean = 2.0 bpm, p = 0.098). The active and passive binders

thus elicit significantly greater reductions in ΔHR compared to control, with a slightly

greater effect demonstrated by the active binder.

*Fig. 5c (brown) shows pairwise differences in standing heart rate: control vs. active*

(mean difference = 5.5 bpm, p = 0.001), control vs. passive (mean = 3.3 bpm, p = 0.40),

and passive vs. active (mean = 2.2 bpm, p = 0.01). The active binder thus reduces standing

HR more effectively than either control or passive compression, the latter of which does

not significantly lower standing HR from control.

Supplementary Figs. 1-2 demonstrate that the passive condition elevated both

supine and standing heart rate relative to control conditions.

## Discussion

In this study, we demonstrated that a portable, motorized active abdominal binder

can deliver precise, consistent compression pressures, resulting in attenuated orthostatic

tachycardia in healthy subjects. The active binder maintained equivalent or improved user

comfort and ease of donning across pressure ranges, addressing critical barriers to real-

world adherence.

Active Binder Design

In this pilot study of twenty healthy adults, our novel active abdominal binder

design successfully meets its technical objectives of portability, minimal bulk, comfort,

and rapid compression. While many traditional compression systems require stationary,

external pump units and are unsuitable for ambulatory use, our device integrates all

actuation and control components for portable use. The slim form factor and < 0.3 kg

weight mitigates the risk that portability comes at the cost of increased wearer burden. As

a point of reference, back braces commonly weigh approximately 0.3 to 0.4 kg, indicating

that the device is in a reasonable weight range. The compact electronics system also

eliminated the need for an external electronics pouch, a characteristic that other solutions

require and may impede usability [22].

Beyond portability and lightness, our binder achieves its target pressure in under 7

seconds, significantly faster than existing pneumatic devices that can require up to 30

seconds to inflate [22]. Multiple studies have demonstrated that rapid onset of compression

is likely critical for reducing orthostatic symptoms and countering the abrupt hemodynamic

shifts that occur upon standing [25, 26]. Moreover, this fast-acting mechanism opens


<!-- Page 34 -->


33

avenues for more advanced control strategies, such as intermittent or more advanced

feedback-adaptive compression, which would be impractical with slower inflation systems.

Should faster actuation be required in future iterations, the modular motor architecture

allows straightforward upgrades: motors with higher RPM (at the expense of torque),

additional winding spools, or optimized gear ratios could achieve the desired improvement.

The automated compression mechanism in our active binder, which detects the

wearer’s transition to standing via the integrated IMU, offers hands-free operation and

limits compression to moments of orthostatic stress. By engaging only when rising motion

is sensed, the device avoids unnecessary abdominal pressure during periods of supine or

seated rest, a significant advantage over patient-controlled inflation systems that rely on

users to manually activate compression before each stand [20].

Compression Pressure

Our results demonstrate that the active binder achieved a higher mean compression

pressure than the maximum passive binder pressures, by around 2 mmHg (despite

participants being instructed to “tighten as much as possible”) and did so with greater

consistency. In the active system, pressure control software halts motor winding once the

target is reached, whereas the passive binder reflects an individual’s maximal voluntary

tightening. Consequently, if clinical needs dictate higher compression levels, the active

device’s setpoint can be readily increased without hardware changes.

Variability analysis further underscores this advantage. The active binder exhibited

roughly half the variability of the passive system according to standard deviation and IQR,


<!-- Page 35 -->


34

indicating more consistent achievement of target pressure. Analyses revealed that, with the

passive binder, males generated higher pressures than females and larger waists correlated

with greater compression. It is important to note that sex and abdominal size are

interdependent, and therefore the individual effects of each must be taken into

consideration. The multiple linear regression suggested statistically significant differences

based on abdominal size while keeping sex constant, but insignificant differences based on

sex for a given abdominal size. Note that p-values are reported, instead of R2, because the

question of interest is whether the slope should be considered nonzero. The result suggests

that the sex-based variability in passive pressure observed may be attributed to differences

in abdominal size, rather than sex independently.

In any case, this result is significant, as passive binders may be susceptible to

greater variability; in real‐world settings, factors such as age‐related strength decline [16,

27] or reduced device familiarity could exacerbate inconsistency. Future work could

investigate these factors in greater detail.

By contrast, the active binder’s closed‐loop control and straightforward donning

protocol minimize user‐dependent variability. This consistency may be critical for

predictable hemodynamic support across diverse patient populations.

The target compression pressure of approximately 11 mmHg was selected to

balance hemodynamic efficacy with comfort and safety during sustained use. Prior studies

have indicated that external abdominal pressures exceeding about 12 mmHg may become

uncomfortable or unsafe for prolonged wear [28-30]. The higher pressures (20–40 mmHg)

reported in the literature generally refer to internal bladder inflation pressures [21, 22],


<!-- Page 36 -->


35

which have been shown to overestimate the true external compression experienced by the

abdomen due to tension within the bladders [30]. In contrast, the present device applies

compression through direct mechanical contraction, producing an accurately measured

external pressure. Thus, despite differing nominal values, the effective abdominal

compression achieved in this study is likely comparable to that of previously reported

systems.

Previous work also suggests that the area of applied compression may be more

influential for hemodynamic support than absolute pressure magnitude [31]. The active

binder engaged most of the abdominal surface area, thereby providing effective coverage

in this regard. Future work could systematically investigate how variations in compression

force within the ~11 mmHg range influence hemodynamic response, to better define the

optimal balance between efficacy and comfort.

The optimal duration for sustained abdominal compression also remains unknown.

Prior studies have typically assessed responses over short intervals (≤ 3 minutes) [20, 21,

31], and longer-term physiological or comfort effects have not been systematically

evaluated. In the absence of evidence supporting gradual decompression, the current device

applies continuous pressure while standing to ensure stable hemodynamic support. The

hemodynamic response to compression is likely patient-specific, varying with the degree

of autonomic dysfunction and vascular tone. The active binder allows for individualized

programming of pressure trajectories, enabling adjustments such as gradual pressure

reduction or variable target pressures to optimize support for different patient profiles.


<!-- Page 37 -->


36

The design of the pressure measurement system also warrants further discussion.

Our binder applies a flat pressure on the front of the abdomen, concentrating compression

over the abdominal venous reservoir and minimizing pressure on the hips and ribs. The

small pressure bladder, positioned directly beneath the flat compression region, was

designed to measure local average pressure. Prior to testing, this design was evaluated in

comparison with direct contact-based transducers, which yielded variable readings due to

inconsistent apposition and shear. Additionally, since the same pressure measurement

approach was used for both active and passive binders, relative comparisons are preserved

even if a systematic bias exists.

Physiological Efficacy

Our findings demonstrate that the active abdominal binder attenuates orthostatic

tachycardia by ~5 bpm according to both ΔHR and standing HR. The passive binder

achieves slightly less improvement, especially when examining the standing heart rate

response. Although data on heart rate modulation in healthy cohorts are scarce, one prior

study reported a 5 – 7 bpm decrease in standing tachycardia with a passive abdominal

binder versus no compression [24]. Discrepancies between their results and ours may stem

from differences in donning protocols, investigator assistance during application, or

participant demographics and physiology. Despite modest effect sizes in this healthy

population, our data provide a compelling proof‐of‐concept that active abdominal

compression can mitigate orthostatic heart rate surges.

The differing results between ΔHR and standing HR for the passive condition merit

further consideration. The modest elevation in supine heart rate observed with the passive


<!-- Page 38 -->


37

binder likely reflects slight sympathetic activation or discomfort during manual donning,

which in turn may blunt its apparent efficacy at higher pressures (as seen in Fig. 6).

Clinically, standing heart rate may be the more meaningful endpoint, since orthostatic

intolerance is predominantly driven by blood pressure and preload demands rather than

baseline variations in healthy individuals. Nonetheless, the active binder consistently

lowered both ΔHR and standing HR relative to control.

Multiple linear regression demonstrated that the active mechanism provides an

additional ~4.4 bpm reduction in standing heart rate beyond what pressure alone would

predict. The results of the regression and the trends observed in Fig. 6 suggest a possible

intrinsic advantage of the active mechanism beyond simply delivering higher pressures.

One potential explanation is that continuous preload from a passive binder while supine

may evoke parasympathetic compensation, blunting its efficacy upon standing [20, 32, 33];

the active binder, by only engaging during upright posture, may avoid this adjustment and

therefore elicit more pronounced orthostatic support. However, given the paucity of prior

comparative studies between passive and active binders and our modest sample size, this

hypothesis remains preliminary. Future research with matched pressure setpoints between

the active and passive conditions and larger cohorts will be needed to clarify the

mechanistic underpinnings of active and passive compression.

Furthermore, it is reasonable to expect not only greater benefits of compression

devices but also a more meaningful comparison of compression mechanism in patients with

POTS or OH, whose baseline autonomic compensations are impaired, consistent with


<!-- Page 39 -->


38

previous studies [15, 34, 35]. These results lay the groundwork for subsequent trials in

clinical populations.

It is important to note that the clinical management of OH and POTS differ [36],

and so implementation of this compression technology may be specific to patient

populations. Despite these differences, compression therapy has been demonstrably

effective at treating both OH and POTS [13], and the underlying mechanism (limiting

splanchnic venous capacitance) has relevance for both pathologies.

User Comfort

Survey data (Table 2) indicate that participants found the active binder at least as

comfortable as the passive system across all eight prompts, with the most pronounced

advantage noted during supine rest. As expected, higher compression pressures correlated

with modest declines in comfort and breathing ease (Fig. 8), highlighting an inherent trade-

off between hemodynamic support and wearability. Nevertheless, the active binder

maintained comfort ratings equivalent to, or above, those of the passive device at each

pressure level and, due to its programmable setpoints, offers the ability to finely tune this

balance on a per-patient basis.

Ease of donning emerged as another crucial differentiator. Unlike the passive

binder, which participants had to tighten manually under load, the active system only needs

to be “snug” at baseline, after which motorized actuation delivers full compression. This

simplified application not only drove higher ease-of-use scores (4.4 vs. 4.0) but also

mitigates a major barrier to real-world adherence: difficulty putting on the garment. Poor


<!-- Page 40 -->


39

adherence, reported at 30–50% for lower-limb compression stockings and even higher for

abdominal binders, is attributed to both donning challenges and discomfort [13, 16, 37].

Many current approaches to adaptive abdominal compression rely on the user

manually pulling straps or activating an inflation mechanism immediately before standing

[20, 38]. These methods may further compromise usability and adherence, since they place

the burden of timing and execution entirely on the wearer.

By allowing for automatic compression and donning at low tension, the active

binder may have the potential to improve long-term compliance and broaden clinical

adoption.

## Limitations

Device Limitations

The current prototype employs felt for the base layer, chosen for ease of fabrication

but not optimized for long-term wear; future iterations could substitute minimally

extensible foam or medical-grade padding to improve comfort. Although the test unit

withstood over 200 compression cycles without failure, the cords, grommets, and fabric

channels remain potential wear points. Future designs could incorporate low-friction nylon

cords or pulley-based guides to reduce abrasion. More rigorous testing of device durability

and battery life are required. The Velcro-mounted blood pressure bladder pouch was a

temporary solution and replacing it with a permanently sealed, leak-resistant housing

would reduce maintenance and prevent sensor displacement. The present prototype is not

programmed for decompression upon sitting or activity (such as walking). Future iterations


<!-- Page 41 -->


40

could include more advanced sensing and control to adjust or release pressure in response

to posture or movement. Finally, the prototype lacks intuitive user-feedback features (e.g.,

LEDs or haptic alerts) to confirm proper donning, battery status, or component faults;

adding simple interface elements will be crucial for independent use outside the laboratory.

Study Limitations

Since we enrolled only healthy adults with intact autonomic function, our results

do not directly demonstrate efficacy in POTS or OH patients whose baroreflex sensitivity

and vascular tone are compromised. While heart rate is generally a strong proxy for

orthostatic stress, future studies should incorporate ambulatory blood pressure

measurements or ultrasound‐based assessments of venous return. The supine-to-standing

transitions used here introduce variability in timing and effort; a tilt-table protocol could

better standardize postural changes and enable exploration of intermediate angles.

Although baseline supine HR differed minimally between conditions and trial order was

randomized, hemodynamic effects during binder donning and potential cumulative effects

across sessions could still have mildly influenced heart rate results. As compression

pressure distribution can be influenced by differences in body habitus, future studies and

design refinements will be necessary to address this potential variability. Comfort and

usability ratings, while informative, are inherently subjective and may differ based on age,

gender, or other factors; larger, more diverse cohorts and objective wearability metrics are

needed to validate these findings. Future studies will require longer term, standardized

safety evaluations.


<!-- Page 42 -->


41

Future Directions

Given the promising performance of this exploratory device, several important

avenues for future work emerge. The most immediate next step is the completion of a

clinical study involving patients diagnosed with orthostatic hypotension (OH) and postural

orthostatic tachycardia syndrome (POTS). While the present study provides initial

validation of the device’s feasibility, future clinical testing will be critical to more

rigorously evaluate both hemodynamic efficacy and user comfort in comparison to existing

standard-of-care solutions, such as passive abdominal binders. Beyond replicating and

extending these comparisons in a patient population, this next phase of work is designed to

address several key mechanistic and translational questions that remain unresolved.

One central question is determining the minimum compression level required to

reliably alleviate symptoms. Identifying this threshold is particularly important because it

directly informs both device design and clinical usability: if effective symptom relief can

be achieved at lower pressure levels, the device can be optimized for improved comfort,

reduced power consumption, and extended wearability.

A related question is whether the magnitude of applied pressure produces a graded

physiological response, or whether there exists a threshold beyond which additional

compression yields diminishing returns. Understanding this relationship is essential for

optimizing control strategies, as it may enable more precise tailoring of compression

profiles to individual patients. It also has implications for personalization, as different

patients may exhibit varying sensitivities to compression depending on the underlying

etiology of their condition.


<!-- Page 43 -->


42

Another critical and currently unanswered question is whether compression must

be maintained continuously throughout the duration of standing, or whether it can be safely

reduced or removed after an initial stabilization period. This distinction has significant

practical implications. If continuous compression is required, the device must sustain

prolonged actuation, increasing energy demands, mechanical wear, and the potential

consequences of device failure. In contrast, if transient compression during the initial

orthostatic transition is sufficient to stabilize hemodynamics, the device could operate

intermittently, substantially improving battery life, reliability, and overall usability. At

present, there is limited evidence to guide this question, making it a key focus of future

investigation.

To address these gaps, a clinical study involving 30 patients with OH and POTS is

currently being developed, with 10 participants already pre-enrolled. This study will

expand upon the current experimental framework by incorporating a broader range of

compression conditions, including multiple pressure levels and varying durations of

compression application. By systematically varying these parameters, the study aims to

generate a more comprehensive understanding of how both pressure magnitude and

temporal dynamics influence physiological outcomes and symptom relief. These efforts

will be essential for translating the current prototype into a clinically viable and adoptable

therapeutic device.


<!-- Page 44 -->


43

## Conclusion

These findings suggest that active abdominal compression may serve as a more

efficacious, consistent, and user-friendly alternative to passive binders for mitigating

orthostatic intolerance. In contrast to existing approaches, which rely on static compression

that is difficult to titrate and often uncomfortable for prolonged use, the adaptive nature of

this system enables targeted support during physiologically relevant moments, such as

transitions to upright posture. This is particularly important given the complex and

heterogeneous nature of orthostatic intolerance, where symptoms arise from a dynamic

interplay of cardiovascular, autonomic, and vascular factors that are not adequately

addressed by one-size-fits-all interventions.

This work represents a big step toward a practical solution for patients with

orthostatic intolerance by demonstrating the feasibility and potential advantages of an

adaptive abdominal compression system that responds to the physiological demands of

standing. In the absence of effective solutions, many patients continue to experience

recurrent dizziness and syncope, leading to functional impairment, reduced mobility, and,

in vulnerable populations, devastating falls that can result in serious injury and diminished

quality of life. With further validation and refinement, this work has the potential to provide

a practical solution to a critical unmet need, ultimately improving the day-to-day lives of

patients living with orthostatic intolerance.
